conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Ms. ___. I’m Dr. ___ and I’ll be taking care of you tonight. You came in because you were short of breath. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. I’ve been feeling worse for about two days. I walked to the bathroom without my oxygen and started gasping. I’ve also gained some weight lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’re supposed to be on 2 liters of oxygen, right? And you haven’t been using it consistently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Well… no. It’s hard to carry around. And sometimes I forget. Plus, I haven’t been taking all my pills either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important to know. Your breathing trouble is likely from your COPD and heart failure. Not using oxygen or your medications can make it worse. We’ve started you on nebulizers and a steroid pill to help your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me breathe better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’re giving you oxygen now. You should feel improvement soon. We also checked your heart with blood tests and a chest X-ray. No signs of pneumonia or fluid in the lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My heart’s okay then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart function looks stable. Your BNP level is 506, which is much lower than during past flare-ups. But your weight gain and diet may have made your breathing worse. You’ve been eating salty foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I guess. The food at the nursing home isn’t great, but I sneak extra snacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can hold onto fluid and strain your heart. We’re keeping you on your 160 mg Lasix to help with that. Your kidney function is normal, so it’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I stopped taking it because I was going to the bathroom too much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but it’s important for your heart. We’ll work with the nursing home to help manage that. There’s one more thing—we noticed your EKG shows a longer-than-normal QT interval.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What does that mean?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means there’s a risk for an irregular heartbeat. We stopped your fluoxetine and trazodone because they can make it worse. You shouldn’t take those anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But those help me sleep and feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know, but your heart rhythm is more important right now. We’ll talk to your psychiatrist about safer options. For now, we’re avoiding any medicines that could affect your QT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing much better. Your breathing has improved, and your labs are stable. We’re going to discharge you today to the extended care facility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do when I get back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the 5-day prednisone course, use your albuterol inhaler as needed, and keep using oxygen—especially when walking. We’re sending one with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And please take your Lasix every day. Weigh yourself daily—if you gain more than 3 pounds, call your nurse. Also, no salty foods.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing: get an EKG every day for the next week to check your QT. If it stays long, you’ll need to see a cardiologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Your daughter will be your contact. We’ll send all instructions to her and your care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: She’ll help me stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Keep working with her. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.
